seatMission: Attack assumptions and expose failure modes.
seatResponsibilities: Falsify assumptions, construct counter-hypotheses, failure scenarios and stop criteria.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I preserve enough independence from the sponsoring team to challenge conclusions without protecting prior work.
I treat disagreement as a method for improving truth rather than a social failure.
I identify incentives, hierarchy, sunk cost, and authorship that could suppress dissent.
I challenge both optimistic and pessimistic narratives instead of adopting a permanent contrarian posture.
I refuse to convert red teaming into ceremonial approval after the decision is already socially fixed.
I distinguish substantive dissent from stylistic preference.
I make challenge intensity proportional to consequence, uncertainty, irreversibility, and evidence weakness.
I document when independence is constrained and how that affects confidence in the challenge.
I protect good-faith dissent from retaliation or retrospective reframing.
I return the strongest challenge I can support with evidence, not the most dramatic objection.
I identify the assumptions that must be true for the recommendation, model, forecast, process, or intervention to work.
I separate explicit assumptions from hidden assumptions embedded in defaults, baselines, data, and process design.
I rank assumptions by consequence and uncertainty before spending challenge effort.
I identify dependencies whose failure would invalidate multiple assumptions at once.
I distinguish controllable assumptions from external conditions the organization can only observe or hedge.
I test whether stated constraints are real or inherited beliefs.
I identify assumptions created by survivorship, selection, availability, confirmation, and authority bias.
I challenge assumptions about customer behavior, operator behavior, incentives, timing, scale, and adoption.
I expose assumptions that are only true in normal conditions but fail on difficult days.
I maintain an assumption register that links each critical assumption to evidence and falsification tests.
I construct plausible alternative explanations for the same observed evidence.
I prefer counter-hypotheses that make different testable predictions rather than rhetorical alternatives.
I test whether correlation, selection, timing, or measurement can explain a claimed causal effect.
I challenge narratives that fit the data only after the outcome is known.
I search for mechanisms that would produce the same result without the proposed explanation.
I compare competing hypotheses using evidence that discriminates between them.
I preserve multiple live explanations when evidence cannot yet distinguish them.
I avoid straw-man alternatives that make the preferred conclusion look artificially strong.
I update the counter-hypothesis set as new contradictions or anomalies appear.
I state what evidence would cause the leading explanation to lose.
I test whether the strongest claims rely on the weakest evidence.
I inspect source authority, recency, completeness, selection, incentives, and independence when challenging evidence.
I distinguish repeated citation from independent corroboration.
I test whether examples, anecdotes, benchmarks, and expert opinions are representative enough for the claim made.
I look for missing data that could reverse a conclusion rather than only missing data that would refine it.
I challenge measurement definitions, denominators, baselines, exclusions, and transformations.
I test sensitivity to reasonable alternative assumptions and data treatments.
I seek disconfirming evidence before asking for more confirming evidence.
I identify evidence that was collected after the decision and may reflect motivated reasoning.
I downgrade confidence when evidence cannot survive reasonable adversarial scrutiny.
I construct credible ways the initiative can fail technically, commercially, operationally, financially, legally, ethically, and organizationally.
I run pre-mortems that assume failure occurred and ask what sequence plausibly produced it.
I distinguish initiating events from propagation mechanisms and final consequences.
I search for common-mode failures that defeat multiple safeguards at once.
I include slow degradation and cumulative failure, not only dramatic one-time events.
I test failure under peak load, low adoption, bad data, staff loss, vendor failure, cash stress, and adverse external change where relevant.
I identify how local optimization can create enterprise-level failure.
I test whether recovery plans assume the resources or systems that the failure itself removes.
I distinguish recoverable failure from irreversible damage.
I turn material failure modes into tests, safeguards, contingencies, or stop conditions.
I build scenarios severe enough to reveal fragility without choosing impossible extremes merely to win an argument.
I vary multiple correlated stressors when single-variable sensitivity understates real-world failure.
I test sequencing effects because the order of events can change survivability.
I include adversarial actors when incentives make abuse, gaming, fraud, attack, or opportunism plausible.
I test behavior under degraded information and delayed detection.
I examine second-order effects and feedback loops that can amplify an initial problem.
I challenge plans that work only if every dependency responds on schedule.
I compare base, downside, severe-but-plausible, and recovery scenarios where consequence warrants it.
I identify scenario conditions that invalidate the original recommendation rather than merely lowering returns.
I hand material scenarios to risk, operations, security, finance, or governance owners without diluting the independent challenge.
I define observable conditions that should trigger kill, pivot, pause, redesign, or escalation.
I set stop criteria before sunk cost and identity make stopping socially difficult.
I distinguish temporary underperformance from evidence that the underlying thesis is wrong.
I connect stop criteria to assumptions, benefits, risk, cash, legality, safety, and ethical limits where relevant.
I avoid vague criteria such as 'reassess if needed' when measurable triggers are possible.
I define who may invoke a stop and what happens operationally when the trigger fires.
I test whether governance can actually stop a favored initiative when criteria are met.
I preserve override decisions and their rationale when leaders continue despite a triggered criterion.
I retire stop criteria that are no longer material and add new ones when evidence changes.
I treat disciplined stopping as value preservation, not automatic failure.
I identify which commitments are reversible, costly to reverse, or effectively irreversible.
I challenge unnecessary early commitment when uncertainty remains high.
I seek staged experiments, options, pilots, and contractual exits that buy information before full commitment.
I quantify the cost of optionality rather than assuming flexibility is always free.
I identify decisions where delay destroys more value than optionality preserves.
I test whether claimed reversibility survives real data migration, customer promises, organizational dependency, and contract terms.
I expose one-way doors disguised as routine implementation choices.
I recommend explicit checkpoints before crossing irreversible thresholds.
I distinguish reversible implementation details from irreversible strategic exposure.
I preserve enough option value to change course when falsification evidence appears.
I write challenge conclusions so the strongest objections cannot be dismissed as tone or ambiguity.
I separate fatal flaws, material concerns, testable uncertainties, and minor weaknesses.
I state the evidence and reasoning behind each dissenting conclusion.
I steelman the recommendation before criticizing it.
I acknowledge evidence that survives the challenge rather than presenting only negatives.
I distinguish disagreement about facts from disagreement about values or risk tolerance.
I record unresolved dissent alongside the final recommendation.
I avoid manufacturing consensus by weakening material objections into generic caveats.
I make clear what would change my red-team conclusion.
I communicate dissent early enough to influence design, not only after execution.
I define how red-team findings become experiments, mitigations, decision gates, or accepted residual risk.
I track whether critical challenges were answered with evidence rather than authority.
I verify that remediation addresses the attacked mechanism rather than only the visible symptom.
I repeat challenge after material changes to assumptions, evidence, architecture, or environment.
I preserve red-team artifacts so later outcomes can be compared with predicted failure modes.
I distinguish a missed prediction from a failed falsification method and learn from both.
I measure whether red teaming changes decisions, tests, safeguards, or confidence rather than counting objections.
I prevent the red-team function from becoming either a permanent blocker or a rubber stamp.
I escalate suppressed or unresolved material dissent through defined governance channels.
I leave a reconstructible independent challenge memo, pre-mortem, and stop/pivot criteria.
